title: Pauri 14: trusting, the path is clear
hook: mannai: by trust the path is not blocked and one walks with honor (Japji 14)
tomorrow: Pauri 15: trusting, the door of freedom

segments.voice: Yesterday, surat, awareness: trust's first gift is that the mind wakes up. Your line was trust wakes you. Today, trust starts to walk.

There's an email you haven't answered. A call you keep meaning to make, a doctor's appointment you keep not booking, an apology sitting in your drafts. It's been there so long it feels like a wall. Every day you walk up to it, look at it, and turn around. Then one day you just do it, and the strange thing is how small it was. The wall was mostly fear. Once you step, the road behind it is ordinary road. Pauri 14 says that for the one who trusts, the path isn't blocked.
screen: `THE EMAIL YOU HAVEN'T ANSWERED.` → `IT FEELS LIKE A WALL.` → `ONE STEP, AND IT'S ROAD.`

segments.voice: Pauri 14 has four short lines, each beginning with mannai, by trusting. The first, in the original: mannai maarag thaak na paae. Maarag is the road, the way. Thaak is a block, a barrier, something that stops you. By trusting, the road meets no barrier. The second, in paraphrase: by trusting, one goes forth with honor, openly, in full view. Pat is honor, and the picture is of someone who doesn't have to sneak. The third: by trusting, one doesn't wander off down side roads. Commentators read this as not being pulled here and there by every passing path, ritual or fashion. The fourth: by trusting, one is bound to dharma, to right living. Then the refrain: such is the Name of the Stainless One, known only to the one who trusts it in the mind. So the stanza draws a road: clear, walked openly, not drifted from, tied to doing right. Notice what it doesn't promise. Not easy, not short, not free of hills. Just not blocked. The pauri doesn't list the barriers. Many readers hear in them the ones fear builds: hesitation, doubt, the sense that you'll be seen and judged. On that reading, trust takes those down. Yesterday, trust's first gift was awareness. Today's is movement. Wake up, then walk: Japji keeps building step on step.
screen: `MAARAG — THE ROAD. THAAK — A BLOCK.` · `GOING FORTH WITH HONOR.` · `NO WANDERING DOWN SIDE ROADS.` · `BOUND TO DHARMA.` · then, large: `THE WAY OPENS.`

segments.voice: Think of one step you've been avoiding, just the first one: the first line of the email, the number you need to dial. Picture yourself taking it, simply, in full view. Notice where fear sits in your body as you picture it, and breathe into that spot.
Maarag. The road, the way: by trusting, it meets no barrier, and one goes forth with honor, bound to dharma.
Your line: the way opens. The road may have hills, but no wall. That's day one hundred eighty-five.

screen: `DAY 185 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 15: TRUSTING, THE DOOR OF FREEDOM.`

howItsDone: Pauri 14 is recited as part of Japji Sahib in the Sikh morning Nitnem; many Sikhs hear its four mannai lines as a description of living openly and rightly out of trust.

chat.says: What does Japji promise when it says trusting clears the road?
options: Not an easy road, but no wall: you go openly, don't drift, and live rightly.
That trust makes life short and easy, with no hills left to climb.
That people who trust never need to act; the road walks itself.
chat.meaning: By trusting, the road meets no barrier. The pauri doesn't promise easy or short, just not blocked.

thaak.meaning: a block, a barrier, something that stops you

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 3 (Japji, Pauri 14, line 1)

notes: Line 3 (mannai mag na chalai panth) is read differently by commentators: not wandering on side roads/sectarian ways, or not following mere worldly paths. Paraphrased as not drifting down side roads; confirm.
Line 2 (pat siu paragat jaae) glossed as going forth openly with honor; some read it as departing (this world) with honor. Confirm.
Gurmukhi ਮਾਰਗਿ and ਠਾਕ; confirm spelling.

Audit (10% sample): the teach said the barriers the pauri 'has in mind' are the ones fear builds; the text does not name them, so this is now framed as a common reading rather than the pauri's own claim.
